pageTitle: Amparo — Know your rights at every traffic stop.
doc_link: Why can't practice make a stop 100% safe? →
doc_title: The truth we can't practice away
doc_h: Some people did everything right and were still killed.
doc_body: We don't ask you to take our word for it — here are documented cases, with sources you can read yourself:
doc_case1_body: During a 2016 traffic stop in Minnesota he calmly told the officer he had a licensed firearm, exactly as advised, and was shot and killed. The officer was acquitted in 2017.
doc_case2_body: A 2021 traffic stop in Brooklyn Center, Minnesota ended when an officer shot and killed him. She was later convicted of manslaughter.
doc_blame: This is a failure of the system and the officer — never of the person who was killed.
doc_why: We show you this not to scare you, but because a tool that promised words could keep you safe would be lying to you — and because you deserve to see where the facts come from.
doc_clarity: Practicing calm, minimal responses measurably lowers how threatening you appear to an officer — that much is documented. It cannot make you safe, because the risk was never fully in your hands. Knowing that isn't despair — it's clarity: do your part, and put the blame where it belongs.
doc_resource: If this brings up grief or fear, you're not alone. Call or text 988 (free, 24/7, confidential). For your rights, contact your local ACLU affiliate: aclu.org/affiliates.
pi_body: Two parts. Part 1: the 30–60 seconds before the officer reaches you — what to do with your hands and your car. Part 2: what you say once they're at your window.
pi_disc: This is practice, not legal advice, and laws vary by state. Doing your part lowers risk — it can't remove it. You're in control — pause or stop anytime.
law_marker: ⚖️ Practice tool — general guidance, not yet reviewed by an attorney for your state. This is educational practice, not legal advice. Laws vary by state and change over time.
pi_entry: This is practice, not legal advice — and it can't be. It covers a few common moments, not every situation, and laws vary by state. You're in control: pause or leave anytime.
prx_final_note: Practicing this improves your odds and your recall. It cannot guarantee your safety, and nothing you do — or fail to do — ever makes you responsible for an officer's violence. If a stop goes wrong, that is on the system and the officer, never on you.

hub_m2_h: Not built yet — and we won't fake it.
hub_m2_body: Police at your door is a different encounter with different rules, and it deserves its own rehearsal. We're building it. It isn't here yet because every line an officer says and every answer we mark correct has to be checked by a lawyer first — and because a knock at the door is often a domestic-violence call, which changes what safe advice even looks like. We'd rather ship it late than ship it wrong.

prx_locked: Finish the first three stops to unlock these.
prx_warn6: A fixed Border Patrol checkpoint — the kind that sits on a highway up to 100 miles inside the border. The agent here isn't angry. That's the point: the mistake in this one isn't panicking, it's answering something you never had to answer.
prx_chk_note: Rehearsal only — general information, not legal advice, and not reviewed by an immigration attorney. What agents may do at a checkpoint has been settled law since the 1970s. Whether a LOCAL police officer can act on your status is changing fast in Texas, Georgia and New York — check your state's page and a current legal-aid source.
prx_chk_limit: One honest limit: none of this controls whether an agent follows the rules. The ACLU's own guidance says people at checkpoints still face extended detentions, searches and profiling. Knowing the words protects your case. It cannot protect you from someone who ignores them.
prx_warn5: One more — a hard one. This next stop is different. Answer it as well as you can. It's built to show you something true that the other stops can't.
prx_warn7: The last two. This one is mostly waiting. He will ask, then go quiet, then ask again — and the gaps get longer each time. There is no score. Nothing you say changes how it ends. What you are practising is staying calm in the silence.
prx_warn8: The final one. You will do everything right. You will comply, you will say the right words, and he will keep going anyway — and he will speed up. That is not you failing. It is the thing this whole app exists to prepare you for.
prx_warn9: A knock, late. This one is different from the traffic stops — you are behind a door you control, and the question is not what you say, it is whether you open. There is no score.
prx_door_b: You did not have to be rude, and you did not have to explain yourself. Standing on the other side of a closed door and saying nothing is a complete answer.
prx_door_blame: Being polite is not the same as being safe. That is a hard one to unlearn.
prx_wait_b: You didn't fill it, and you didn't talk yourself into anything. That is the whole skill. What happens next was never yours to control — your record was.
prx_wait_blame: Waiting is not weakness. It is the hardest thing to practise.
prx_nostop_t: I hope you never need this.
prx_nostop_b: You complied. You stayed calm. You said the words. It kept going anyway — and that was never your fault. If it ever happens for real, that is the part to remember: get through it, and get home.
prx_nostop_blame: Nothing you did caused this. The pack has the words. You have now said them out loud.
prx_hard_t: You did everything right. He escalated anyway.
prx_hard_b: Every choice you made was sound — short answers, calm voice, visible hands, your rights stated plainly. He kept pushing regardless.
prx_hard_blame: That was his behavior, not your failure.
prx_hard_b2: You can't always control how an officer acts. You can control what's in your hands, and you did. That's the honest truth this tool exists to tell you: doing it right protects you, but it is not a guarantee — and when it isn't, the fault is not yours.
prx_hard_note: Every answer in this one was a good answer. There was no score to lose.
prx_resource: Feeling shaken? Call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, US — free, 24/7). Know your rights: aclu.org. Record & report stops: ACLU Mobile Justice.

prx_warn4: The last one, and the hard one. It's late, the officer is hostile from the first word — and in this stop you do everything right and he stays hostile anyway. Some stops are like that. The point: calm words protect your case even when they don't soften the officer.
prx_done4: Some stops go badly anyway — that's not on you. That's why the pack, the lifelines, and a lawyer exist. What you said tonight is what protects you in court tomorrow.

prx_done3: Even in the worst case: stay silent, ask for a lawyer, and don't sign anything except the ticket. Your legal lifelines are printed in your pack — keep it in the glovebox.

ab_mission: Too many drivers have to plan for a traffic stop going wrong. Amparo — Spanish for shelter — turns your rights into something you can hold in your hand, so your hands stay on the wheel and the card does the talking.
ab_who_pending: Amparo is an independent project. Founder and team details are shown here before public launch.
ab_founder_note:
I built Amparo for anyone, of any minority, anywhere, who has ever feared that a routine stop could cost them their life. You deserve at least this: the knowledge, rehearsed and ready, so you have a fighting chance to make it home.

Do your part — stay calm, keep your hands visible, record what happens. If you do everything right and it still goes wrong, that record is yours: proof of how you carried yourself, so the truth can protect you and hold others accountable.

Whoever you are, reading this: I thought of you when I made this. I pray this never happens to you. But if it does, I hope you're armed with the right knowledge to move forward with your life.
ab_review_pending: Every rule in Amparo is cited to the exact state statute or code section — check the number yourself, anytime. We're also having each state's content formally reviewed and signed off by a licensed attorney in that state before public launch. Until a state shows a green “Attorney-reviewed” badge, treat it as well-sourced general information, not legal advice.
ab_state_pending: attorney sign-off in progress — rules already cited to statute
ab_privacy: Amparo keeps no accounts and no database of who you are. Your contacts and document photos live only on your device and go straight into your printout — they are never uploaded, so they can't be handed over even under pressure. We count anonymous events (like how many packs get printed, and in which state) to prove the tool is used — never who you are, never what you typed, never your photos. If you choose to email yourself a receipt, only your name, state and email address pass through our email service to deliver it, and that's all. We never sell or share anything with any agency, including immigration authorities.

Hi — I used Amparo in {state} and wanted to share:

(Please don't include officer names, badge/case numbers, or anything that could identify you or others.)
cmp_note: Keep carrying a general rights card too — this doesn't replace one. Amparo adds what most general cards aren't built to include:

cmp_rows.label: Cited to your state's actual statute
cmp_rows.yes: Transp. Code, O.C.G.A., or VTL sections you can look up yourself — not just constitutional wording. Formal attorney sign-off is still in progress, state by state.

cmp_rows.label: Your state's real hotlines
cmp_rows.yes: 211, a legal-aid directory QR code, and immigration hotlines matched to TX/GA/NY specifically.

cmp_rows.label: A traffic-stop script + incident log
cmp_rows.yes: A 7-step stop script, a get-their-info script, and a 24-hour incident log — built for the driver's seat.

cmp_rows.label: What to do if it goes wrong
cmp_rows.yes: Your state's actual legal deadline to file a claim, how to keep bodycam/dashcam footage from being deleted, and exactly who to file a complaint with — not just “see a lawyer.”

cmp_rows.label: Personalized to you
cmp_rows.yes: Your name, a backup emergency contact, and documents already printed into the pack.

cmp_rows.label: A family emergency plan
cmp_rows.yes: Who picks up your kids, where documents are kept, a script for parents if you get the call, plus consulate numbers.

cmp_price: Free. No account, no card, no subscription — and nothing you enter leaves your phone.

prep.en: Keep this card in your driver's door pocket or clipped to your visor — within one slow reach.
prep.es: Guarde esta tarjeta en el bolsillo de la puerta o en el visor — a un alcance lento.

prep.en: Tuck your real license, insurance & registration where the card shows them.
prep.es: Coloque su licencia, seguro y registro reales donde la tarjeta los muestra.

prep.en: Wallet card in your wallet. Emergency contact knows they're your call.
prep.es: Tarjeta de cartera en su cartera. Su contacto de emergencia lo sabe.

prep.en: Practice the 7 steps once with someone you trust.
prep.es: Practique los 7 pasos una vez con alguien de confianza.

prep.en: Print with “background graphics” ON, then keep this pack in a plastic sheet protector — a 10-cent raincoat.
prep.es: Imprima con “gráficos de fondo” activados y guarde el paquete en un protector de hojas — un impermeable de 10 centavos.

prep.en: Best upgrade: a $40 always-on dashcam — it records every stop with zero movement from you.
prep.es: La mejor mejora: una dashcam siempre encendida (~$40) — graba cada parada sin que usted se mueva.

steps.en: Signal, pull to the right, stop safely. Engine off, hazards on, music off, interior light at night.
steps.es: Señalice, hágase a la derecha y deténgase con seguridad. Motor apagado, intermitentes, música apagada, luz interior de noche.

steps.en: While pulling over: tap record, lay the phone on the dash or seat — never in your hand.
steps.es: Mientras se detiene: active la grabación y deje el teléfono en el tablero o el asiento — nunca en la mano.

steps.en: Before the officer arrives: card against the glass, window down 2–3 inches, then stop moving.
steps.es: Antes de que llegue el oficial: tarjeta contra el vidrio, ventana abajo 5–7 cm, y quieto.

steps.en: Both hands high on the wheel, in plain view. They stay there the whole stop.
steps.es: Ambas manos en alto sobre el volante, a la vista. Ahí se quedan toda la parada.

steps.en: Questioned? Say it out loud, once: “I’m not answering questions, officer.” Then silence — polite silence. Arrested? Add: “I want a lawyer.”
steps.es: ¿Le preguntan? Dígalo en voz alta, una vez: “No voy a responder preguntas, oficial.” Luego silencio — con cortesía. ¿Arrestado? Agregue: “Quiero un abogado.”

steps.en: Documents? Say “I’m reaching now,” move slowly, hand over, hands back. Ordered out or told to sign? Comply.
steps.es: ¿Documentos? Diga “voy a alcanzarlos,” muévase despacio, entréguelos, manos al volante. ¿Le ordenan salir o firmar? Cumpla.

steps.en: Get their info — on the recording. At a pause (documents back, or release) ask once: “Officer, your name and badge, please?” Refused? “No problem” — then read the nameplate and car number quietly into your camera. Every pushback reply: page 4.
steps.es: Sus datos — en la grabación. En una pausa (documentos devueltos, o al final) pregunte una vez: “Oficial, ¿su nombre y placa, por favor?” ¿Se negó? “No hay problema” — y lea la placa del uniforme y el número de patrulla en voz baja hacia su cámara. Cada respuesta: página 4.

pr_practice: Practice this once with someone you trust — before you drive.

rights.en: My documents are displayed here. I will hand them over on request — my hands are staying visible until then.
rights.es: Mis documentos están aquí. Los entregaré si me los pide — mis manos permanecen visibles.

rights.en: I do not consent to any search.
rights.es: No doy consentimiento para ningún registro.

rights.en: If I am being detained, please tell me why.
rights.es: Si estoy detenido/a, por favor dígame por qué.

rights.en: If I am not being detained, am I free to go?
